lessons.title: Human Rights, Equality and Freedom of Religion

before.content_html:
Human Rights: A Shared Foundation

In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). Its Article 1 states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Article 18 protects freedom of religion or belief, including the freedom to change religion and to express belief in practice. Religious traditions across the world both shaped and responded to the UDHR — and their teachings on human dignity provide a foundation for much of what is now called human rights thinking.

Key Fact

The UDHR (1948) Article 18 protects freedom of religion or belief. Religious traditions ground human dignity in different ways: Christian teaching cites Genesis 1:27 (humans created in God’s image); Sikhism teaches the complete equality of all through Ik Onkar (“There is one God”); Islam emphasises the dignity God conferred on all humans (Quran 17:70).

Prejudice and Discrimination

Prejudice means forming a negative view of someone without just cause. Discrimination is when prejudice leads to unequal treatment. Religious traditions offer a range of responses to prejudice. Christian teaching holds that all people are made in the image of God — imago Dei — from Genesis 1:27: “God created mankind in his own image.” This teaching is used by many Christians to oppose discrimination in any form. Paul’s letter to the Galatians (3:28) states: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This verse is frequently cited in Christian arguments against racial, gender or social discrimination.

Sikh teaching affirms the complete equality of all human beings. The Mool Mantra (Guru Granth Sahib 1a) opens with Ik Onkar — “There is one God” — from which Sikh teaching derives the oneness of all humanity. Guru Nanak challenged the caste-based prejudice of his era by sitting and eating with people of all social backgrounds, and the langar (community kitchen) at every gurdwara remains a living expression of that principle today. Muslim teaching holds that all people are created equal by Allah; the Prophet Muhammad’s final sermon, delivered at Mecca, is often cited for its teaching that “no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and no non-Arab is superior to an Arab, except by piety and good action.”

The Status and Treatment of Women in Religion

The spec asks students to understand the status and treatment of women in religion — a topic on which different sub-traditions hold significantly different positions. It is important to present each tradition’s actual teaching rather than treating any religion as a single, uniform voice.

Within Christianity, views on women’s roles differ by denomination. The Roman Catholic Church does not ordain women as priests; this position is rooted in the teaching that the priest acts in persona Christi (in the person of Christ). The Church of England, by contrast, voted to ordain women as priests in 1994 and as bishops in 2014. Many evangelical and charismatic Protestant churches ordain women in leadership, while others — drawing on passages such as 1 Timothy 2:12 — restrict certain leadership roles. Quaker (Religious Society of Friends) communities have historically affirmed the equal spiritual authority of women and men since the seventeenth century.

Within Judaism, positions also differ significantly between sub-traditions. Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women as rabbis and maintains a traditional distinction between men’s and women’s roles in worship and communal life. Reform Judaism ordained its first female rabbi in 1972, and Liberal Judaism has done so since 1975. In both Reform and Liberal congregations, women participate fully in all aspects of worship. Contemporary Masorti (Conservative) Judaism has also moved towards ordaining women in many communities.

Within Islam, women lead prayer for female-only congregations in many traditions. Sunni and Shi’a positions on women leading mixed-gender prayer vary. Most mainstream scholarship holds that women do not lead mixed congregations in formal salah, though this has been debated by progressive Muslim scholars. Women have historically been scholars of hadith and Islamic law; figures such as Aisha, the wife of the Prophet, were major religious authorities. In British Muslim communities today, women are increasingly active in mosque leadership, education and community roles.

Sikhism explicitly teaches the complete equality of women and men. The Guru Granth Sahib contains compositions by women, and Sikh teaching has consistently opposed practices that restrict women. In practice, women in Sikh communities lead prayers, read from the Guru Granth Sahib and participate fully in all aspects of gurdwara life. Amritdhari Sikh women undertake the same initiation ceremony (Amrit Sanskar) as men.

A common error is to write “Christianity teaches that women should...” as if all Christians hold the same view. The mark scheme for Theme F explicitly rewards students who name the sub-tradition — Catholic, Anglican, evangelical, Quaker, Reform Jewish, Orthodox Jewish. Each sub-tradition has a distinct position grounded in different readings of scripture and tradition. Top-band answers always name the specific sub-tradition and explain the reasoning behind its view.

The Status and Treatment of LGBTQ+ People in Religion

The spec also asks students to understand the status and treatment of those in same-sex relationships within religion. Again, different sub-traditions hold significantly different views, and those differences are themselves theologically grounded.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches, in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1994), that marriage is a sacrament between a man and a woman. The Church does not recognise same-sex marriage and teaches that same-sex relationships are not in keeping with the natural law as it understands it, while also stating that people with same-sex attractions must be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity. In 2024, Pope Francis approved the blessing of same-sex couples in pastoral contexts, while maintaining the Church’s teaching on marriage itself; this represents a development in pastoral practice, though not a change in doctrine.

Many Protestant and evangelical denominations hold similar teachings to the Catholic Church on marriage, grounding their view in biblical passages including Genesis 2, Romans 1, and 1 Corinthians 6. The Church of England’s official position defines marriage as being between a man and a woman, though debates within the Church are ongoing. The Methodist Church in Britain voted in 2021 to allow same-sex marriages on Methodist premises, reflecting a different reading of Christian teaching. Quaker communities affirmed same-sex marriage as early as 2009. The diversity of Christian positions on this issue is considerable.

Within Judaism, views vary equally significantly. Orthodox Judaism does not permit same-sex marriage. Reform Judaism in Britain and America affirmed same-sex marriage in 1990 and has conducted such ceremonies since. Liberal Judaism (the British Liberal movement) moved to affirm same-sex partnerships earlier still. Masorti communities differ in their approach. Students should understand that Judaism is not monolithic on this question.

Non-religious perspectives, including those of humanist and atheist organisations, generally affirm the equal moral worth and rights of LGBTQ+ people. Humanists UK supports equal marriage and argues from a position that human dignity and happiness are the basis of ethical judgement. The UDHR (Article 2) prohibits discrimination on the basis of “other status”, which many human rights lawyers have interpreted as including sexual orientation.

UDHR Article 18 protects the freedom to hold and express religious beliefs. This includes the freedom to manifest religion through worship, observance, practice and teaching. However, rights come with responsibilities: the UDHR also states that everyone has duties to the community, and that rights may be limited only to protect the rights of others or to meet just requirements of public order. In Britain, the Equality Act 2010 protects religion and belief as a protected characteristic, alongside sexual orientation and gender — meaning that different rights can sometimes come into tension in law and in public life. Religious traditions themselves vary in how they navigate this tension: some emphasise the duty to proclaim one’s faith freely; others emphasise the duty to respect the conscience and dignity of all people.

Key Fact

On women’s ordination: the Roman Catholic Church does not ordain women; the Church of England has ordained women priests since 1994 and women bishops since 2014; Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women rabbis; Reform Judaism has done so since 1972. On same-sex marriage: the Catholic Church does not recognise it; Reform Judaism affirmed it in 1990; the Methodist Church in Britain voted in 2021 to allow same-sex marriages on Methodist premises; Quaker communities affirmed same-sex marriage in 2009. These sub-tradition contrasts are essential for top-band exam answers.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UDHR (1948) provides a secular baseline for human rights, including freedom of religion or belief (Article 18). Religious traditions ground human dignity differently — in imago Dei, in Ik Onkar, in the equality taught by Guru Nanak — but many share the principle that all persons deserve respect.
  • On the status and treatment of women in religion, and the status and treatment of those in same-sex relationships, different sub-traditions hold different views. Named contrasts — Catholic vs Anglican on women’s ordination; Orthodox vs Reform Judaism on women rabbis and same-sex marriage; Quaker vs evangelical Christian on same-sex relationships — are what the mark scheme rewards.
  • Rights and responsibilities come together: the UDHR protects freedom of religious expression alongside other rights. Religious traditions themselves vary in how they understand the balance between proclaiming faith and respecting the dignity of all.
before.exam_tip_html:
The 12-mark Evaluate question on Theme F will give you a statement such as “Religious people cannot support equal rights for LGBTQ+ people” or “All religions treat women equally.” A common error is to treat Christianity — or any religion — as having one single view. The mark scheme explicitly rewards students who name sub-traditions: Catholic, Anglican, Methodist, Quaker, Orthodox Jewish, Reform Jewish. Give arguments FOR the statement (with examples from traditions where that view applies) and arguments AGAINST (with examples from traditions that take a different view). Your JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION must say which side is stronger and why, referring to specific religious teachings. Always include a non-religious perspective (e.g. Humanists UK, the UDHR) alongside religious views. The conclusion must be present — not implied.

For the 6-mark Explain question, remember the source-of-authority requirement. Good sources for this lesson include Genesis 1:27, Galatians 3:28, the Mool Mantra (GGS 1a), the UDHR Article 18, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church. Name the source AND develop it — don’t just list it.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following documents first set out the right to freedom of religion or belief as an internationally recognised human right?
A) The Equality Act 2010
B) The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
C) The Geneva Convention (1949)
D) The European Convention on Human Rights (1950)
practice_questions.marks: B) The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the religious practice at a Sikh gurdwara which expresses the equality of all people through communal eating.
practice_questions.marks: Langar [1 mark]. Accept: community kitchen / free kitchen.

practice_questions.text:
Give two contrasting religious beliefs about the status of women in religious leadership.
Refer to two different religious traditions or sub-traditions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Two contrasting beliefs, each developed:
1 mark for each belief stated; 1 additional mark for development of that belief with reference to a specific tradition or source.
Acceptable examples:
- The Roman Catholic Church teaches that only men may be ordained as priests, grounded in the tradition that the priest acts in persona Christi (1+1).
- The Church of England ordained women priests in 1994 and women bishops in 2014, reflecting a different reading of the equal dignity of all before God (1+1).
- Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women as rabbis, maintaining traditional distinctions in worship roles (1+1).
- Reform Judaism has ordained women rabbis since 1972, applying the principle of equal human dignity (1+1).
- Sikhism explicitly teaches the complete equality of women and men, reflected in women reading the Guru Granth Sahib and leading prayers at gurdwaras (1+1).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some religious people believe they have a duty to speak out against discrimination.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two well-developed reasons, each grounded in a specific religious tradition; at least one named source of religious teaching (e.g. Genesis 1:27 on imago Dei; Galatians 3:28; Mool Mantra GGS 1a; Quran 17:70 on human dignity). Both reasons clearly developed with explanation of why the teaching leads to action against discrimination. Sub-tradition named where relevant.
Secure (3-4): Two reasons present and generally accurate, one with source reference; development present but partial.
Developing (2): One reason developed, or two reasons stated without development; source reference missing or not linked to the argument.
Emerging (1): Basic point stated; little or no religious knowledge; no source.

practice_questions.text:
'No religion can fully support freedom of religion for everyone.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Some religious traditions claim exclusive truth: if one religion is correct, other religions may be seen as mistaken, creating tension with the principle of complete freedom of religious expression.
- Some religious teachings on gender roles or same-sex relationships restrict the full participation of certain groups, which critics argue conflicts with equal rights.
- Historical examples (Inquisitions, religious persecution) show that religiously motivated discrimination against other faiths has occurred.
- Non-religious (humanist) arguments suggest that complete neutrality on religion is easier to achieve from a secular position than from within a particular faith tradition.
Arguments against:
- Most major religious traditions explicitly teach the duty to respect human dignity and the rights of others: Genesis 1:27 (imago Dei), Ik Onkar (Sikhism), the ummah's teaching on human equality in Islam.
- Religious communities have been among the strongest advocates for freedom of religion globally: Quakers were early advocates of religious tolerance; Jewish communities have historically championed freedom of conscience.
- UDHR Article 18 was shaped in part by religious voices; many signatories represented states with established religious traditions.
- Different sub-traditions within Christianity, Judaism and Islam affirm both the equal dignity of all people and the freedom to believe differently.
Non-religious perspectives: Humanists UK and Amnesty International argue that freedom of religion is a universal right that all people — religious or not — can and should support.
Mastering (10-12): Balanced, well-developed argument on both sides; named religious teachings on each side; at least one non-religious perspective; reasoned and supported justified conclusion stating which side is stronger and why.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present and generally accurate; some religious teachings cited; conclusion reached but not fully justified.
Developing (4-6): One-sided argument or both sides present but undeveloped; some religious knowledge but generic; conclusion attempted.
Emerging (1-3): Basic points; little religious knowledge; no conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Priya is a 17-year-old who attends a Reform Jewish synagogue in north London. She has been asked to give a d'var Torah (short teaching) at a Shabbat service. Her Orthodox Jewish cousin tells her this would never happen at his synagogue.
Give two differences between how Orthodox and Reform Judaism approach women's participation in synagogue worship.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid difference, up to 2 marks:
- Orthodox synagogues separate men and women in seating (mechitza); Reform synagogues have mixed seating.
- Orthodox Judaism does not permit women to lead communal prayer or read from the Torah in the same way as men; Reform Judaism allows women to lead all aspects of worship.
- Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women as rabbis; Reform Judaism has done so since 1972.
- In an Orthodox synagogue a woman would not typically give a Torah teaching to a mixed congregation; in a Reform synagogue this is permitted.

knowledge_checks.q: Which article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects freedom of religion or belief?
What does the Latin phrase 'imago Dei' mean, and why is it important in Christian arguments against discrimination?
options: The love of God — used to argue that God loves everyone equally
The image of God — used to argue that all humans share equal dignity as bearers of God's image
The law of God — used to argue that God's commands must be obeyed
The peace of God — used to argue that Christians must promote peace

knowledge_checks.q: The Church of England ordained women as priests in _____ and as bishops in _____.
Reform Judaism affirmed same-sex marriage in _____, making it one of the earliest Jewish denominations to do so.
Match each religious tradition to its teaching on women's ordination or leadership:
right: Does not ordain women as priests
Explicitly teaches the complete equality of women and men
Has ordained women as rabbis since 1972

before.content_html:
What Is Social Justice?

Social justice is the principle that all people in society deserve fair treatment, equal opportunities and access to the resources needed for a dignified life. Religious traditions across the world have produced some of the most sustained arguments for social justice in history — and some of the most powerful social movements for racial equality have been explicitly grounded in religious teaching.

Christian teaching on justice runs through both the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament) and the New Testament. The prophet Amos declared: “Let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream” (Amos 5:24). In the New Testament, Jesus summarised the entire Law as loving God and loving your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:37–39). Catholic Social Teaching — developed through documents such as Rerum Novarum (1891) and Gaudium et Spes (1965) — explicitly states that every person has a right to work, to fair wages and to conditions of dignity. Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 states that the social order must be founded on truth, justice, love and freedom.

Key Fact

Key religious foundations for social justice include: Amos 5:24 (the Hebrew prophetic tradition); Galatians 3:28 (Christian equality); the Jewish concept of tzedek (justice) and tikkun olam (healing the world); the Islamic concept of adl (justice); the Sikh teaching of sewa (service as worship); the Hindu virtue of ahimsa (non-harm). Each tradition connects the pursuit of justice to its central understanding of God, human dignity or right living.

Racial Prejudice and Discrimination

Racial discrimination is the unjust or harmful treatment of people because of their race or ethnicity. Religious traditions have both opposed racial discrimination through their teachings and, at times, been used to justify it — a tension that makes the study of religion and race important for understanding history and contemporary society.

Christian teaching on racial equality has been central to some of the most significant social movements of the twentieth century. The civil rights movement in the United States, led in significant part by the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr, drew explicitly on Christian scripture and theology. King, a Baptist minister, used Paul’s letter to the Galatians and the teachings of Jesus on the dignity of all persons to argue for the complete equality of Black Americans. His “Letter from Birmingham Jail” (1963) argued that Christians had a moral duty to resist unjust laws, drawing on the natural-law tradition rooted in Augustine and Aquinas. King’s vision was of a “beloved community” in which the dignity of every person was recognised regardless of race.

In South Africa, the churches played a significant and contested role in the struggle against apartheid. Archbishop Desmond Tutu — an Anglican bishop and theologian — drew on the Christian teaching of imago Dei and the concept of the ubuntu philosophy (“I am because we are”) to argue that apartheid was not only politically wrong but theologically incompatible with Christianity. Nelson Mandela, though his political framework was broader, similarly drew on the language of human dignity. After apartheid ended in 1994, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, co-chaired by Tutu, drew on Christian concepts of confession, forgiveness and reconciliation.

Islam teaches the equality of all people before Allah. The concept of the ummah — the worldwide community of believers — explicitly transcends racial and national lines. The Prophet Muhammad’s final sermon at Mecca stated that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and no non-Arab superior to an Arab, except through piety. British Muslim organisations including Muslim Aid and the Muslim Council of Britain have made public statements opposing racial discrimination and supporting anti-racist work in Britain.

Jewish teaching on justice is rooted in the concept of tzedek (righteousness and justice) and tikkun olam (“healing the world”). Jewish communities in Britain and the United States were prominent in civil rights movements; many American Jewish organisations supported the civil rights movement alongside Black-led organisations. The Jewish concept of Pikuach Nefesh — that saving a human life overrides almost all other commandments — grounds the principle that every human life has equal infinite value, regardless of background.

Sikh teaching grounds racial equality in the concept of the oneness of humanity expressed through Ik Onkar. Guru Nanak challenged caste-based discrimination in sixteenth-century Punjab, and the langar (community kitchen) at every gurdwara is a practical expression of the teaching that all people are equal. Khalsa Aid, a Sikh humanitarian organisation founded in Britain in 1999, works globally in disaster zones and refugee crises, providing aid regardless of race, religion or background — an expression of the Sikh principle of sewa (selfless service).

Positive Discrimination

Positive discrimination (also called affirmative action) involves giving preferential treatment to members of groups that have historically faced discrimination, with the aim of correcting past injustice and creating greater equality of opportunity. It is a contested policy that raises questions about justice and fairness.

Religious views on positive discrimination vary. Some Christians argue that positive discrimination is consistent with the gospel principle of concern for the vulnerable and marginalised — the “option for the poor” in Catholic Social Teaching, developed in Gaudium et Spes, holds that justice sometimes requires giving particular attention to those who have been most disadvantaged. Other Christians argue that treating people differently because of their race — even to correct past wrongs — conflicts with the principle that all people are equal before God and should be treated as individuals rather than members of a group.

Non-religious ethical arguments also divide on this issue. Those who favour positive discrimination argue from the principle of equality of outcome: if historical discrimination has created structural disadvantage, simply treating everyone “the same” may perpetuate that disadvantage. Those who oppose it argue from the principle of equality of opportunity: people should be judged only on their individual merits, and any policy that judges on group membership may itself be a form of discrimination.

Contemporary Britain provides specific contexts in which religious communities have engaged with questions of racial justice. The Grenfell Tower fire in 2017, in which 72 people died, affected a highly diverse community in west London. Religious communities — including the local mosque, churches and the Notting Hill community — were among the first to respond with practical support. Inquiries into the fire raised questions about how structural inequality, race and poverty intersect in housing policy. The Windrush Scandal, in which British citizens of Caribbean heritage were wrongly detained or deported from 2017 onwards, prompted responses from Church of England bishops and other religious leaders who argued that the dignity of these individuals — many of whom had come to Britain to help rebuild the country after World War Two — demanded immediate redress. These contemporary British examples show how the principles of social justice and racial equality taught by religious traditions continue to be relevant to real events in British life today.

Key Fact

The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr drew on Baptist Christian theology — especially Galatians 3:28 and the concept of the beloved community — in the US civil rights movement. Archbishop Desmond Tutu drew on imago Dei and the ubuntu philosophy in opposing South African apartheid. Both show how religious teaching has directly shaped real-world campaigns for racial justice.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religious traditions ground social justice in key teachings: Christian prophetic tradition (Amos 5:24), Catholic Social Teaching (Gaudium et Spes), Jewish tzedek and tikkun olam, Islamic adl and the ummah, Sikh sewa. Each tradition connects justice to its central theological commitments.
  • Real historical figures — Martin Luther King Jr and Archbishop Desmond Tutu — drew explicitly on religious teaching to oppose racial discrimination. Contemporary UK examples (Grenfell, Windrush) show religious communities continuing to engage with racial justice today.
  • Positive discrimination is contested: some religious and ethical arguments support it as a corrective for structural injustice; others oppose it on the grounds of individual equality. Mark-scheme answers name the specific argument and its grounding rather than stating a preference.
before.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on social justice or racial discrimination, you must refer to a source of religious belief and teaching. Strong sources include: Galatians 3:28 (Christian equality); Amos 5:24 (prophetic justice); the concept of tzedek or tikkun olam (Judaism); the ummah (Islam); Ik Onkar (Sikhism). Name the source AND explain how it grounds the religious argument — don’t just list it. Examiners reward students who develop the link: “Because all humans are made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), Christians argue that racial discrimination is a violation of the dignity that God has conferred on every person.”

For the 12-mark Evaluate on positive discrimination, you must present both sides: those who support it (from the option for the poor in Catholic Social Teaching, or from equality-of-outcome arguments) and those who oppose it (from equal treatment before God as individuals, or from equality-of-opportunity arguments). Include both religious and non-religious perspectives. Your justified conclusion must state which side is stronger and why — it must be present, not implied.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'tikkun olam' in Jewish teaching?
A) The duty to pray three times a day
B) The concept of healing or repairing the world through acts of justice and compassion
C) The traditional Shabbat meal shared with family
D) The belief in life after death
practice_questions.marks: B) The concept of healing or repairing the world through acts of justice and compassion [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the religious principle, used by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, which expresses the interconnectedness of all human beings and was used to oppose apartheid in South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Ubuntu [1 mark]. Accept: 'I am because we are' / the ubuntu philosophy.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some religious believers support positive discrimination as a way of achieving racial equality.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Two reasons, each developed:
1 mark for a reason stated; 1 additional mark for development.
Acceptable examples:
- Catholic Social Teaching's 'option for the poor' teaches that justice sometimes requires giving particular attention to the most disadvantaged; positive discrimination applies this to racial inequality caused by historical discrimination (1+1).
- The principle of tikkun olam (healing the world) in Jewish teaching requires active efforts to repair injustice, not merely treating people equally from this point onwards (1+1).
- If structural discrimination has left particular groups behind, simply treating everyone 'the same' does not achieve equality of outcome; religious teaching on the equal dignity of all may require active correction (1+1).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which religious teaching has led believers to work against racial discrimination.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two well-developed ways, each grounded in a specific named religious teaching. At least one named source (e.g. Galatians 3:28; Genesis 1:27; Amos 5:24; the ummah; Ik Onkar; tzedek). Both developed with clear explanation of how the teaching motivates action against racial discrimination. Sub-tradition or specific tradition named.
Secure (3-4): Two ways present and generally accurate; one with a named source; development present but partial.
Developing (2): One way developed, or two stated without development; source missing or not linked.
Emerging (1): Basic point; little religious knowledge; no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Positive discrimination is the most effective way to tackle racial inequality.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Catholic Social Teaching's 'option for the poor' (Gaudium et Spes) supports policies that actively favour the disadvantaged; this principle can be applied to race.
- The Jewish concept of tikkun olam requires active repair of injustice, not passive non-discrimination.
- Historical data shows that passive equality of opportunity has not corrected racial inequality in employment, housing or education; positive discrimination may be necessary to produce genuine equality of outcome.
- The Islamic teaching that all are equal before Allah (the ummah) may require structural action when structural racism has created inequality.
Arguments against:
- Many Christian traditions argue that all people should be treated equally as individuals before God, and that judging on group membership may itself be a form of discrimination.
- The principle of equality of opportunity holds that people should be assessed on individual merit; positive discrimination can seem to conflict with meritocracy.
- Some argue that positive discrimination can create resentment and does not address the root causes of discrimination.
- Non-religious ethical perspectives (Kantian ethics) argue that treating people as a means to a social end violates their dignity as individuals.
Non-religious perspectives: Humanists UK supports equality of opportunity and anti-discrimination law but is divided on positive discrimination; focus is on challenging prejudice rather than quotas.
Mastering (10-12): Balanced argument both sides; named religious teachings; at least one non-religious view; reasoned justified conclusion with clear reason why one side is stronger.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; some religious teaching; conclusion present but weakly justified.
Developing (4-6): One-sided or both sides undeveloped; generic religious knowledge; conclusion attempted.
Emerging (1-3): Basic points; little religious knowledge; no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Marcus attends a Baptist church in Birmingham. His church has recently started a community project responding to racial inequality in the local area. Give two ways a Christian might respond to racial discrimination, drawing on their faith.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid response, up to 2 marks:
- Campaigning for equal treatment in employment, housing or education, grounded in the teaching that all are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27).
- Participating in community projects that support people of all races, as an expression of loving your neighbour (Matthew 22:39).
- Joining anti-racist organisations or peaceful protest, following the example of Martin Luther King Jr who drew on Christian teaching.
- Challenging racist language or behaviour within their community, grounded in the equal dignity of all before God.

lessons.title: Wealth, Poverty and the Uses of Money

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct definition of 'zakat' in Islam?
A) The voluntary fasting during Ramadan
B) The obligatory annual giving of a portion of savings to those in need, one of the Five Pillars
C) The pilgrimage to Mecca undertaken once in a lifetime
D) The declaration of faith: 'There is no god but Allah'
practice_questions.marks: B) The obligatory annual giving of a portion of savings to those in need, one of the Five Pillars [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Sikh practice of tithing one tenth of one's income for the benefit of the community.
Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about the right attitude to wealth.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Two contrasting beliefs, each developed:
1 mark for a belief stated; 1 additional mark for development with reference to a specific tradition.
Acceptable examples:
- Christian stewardship teaches that wealth belongs ultimately to God; humans are caretakers responsible for using it wisely and sharing with those in need (Genesis 1:28) (1+1).
- Buddhist non-attachment teaches that clinging to wealth is greed (lobha), one of the Three Poisons causing suffering; wealth should be held lightly and shared through dana (1+1).
- Islamic teaching allows the lawful acquisition of wealth but requires zakat (2.5% giving) as a purification and redistribution; wealth concentrated without zakat is condemned (1+1).
- Sikh dasvandh requires giving one tenth of income to the community; the principle of kirat karna insists wealth must be earned honestly (1+1).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why religious believers oppose the charging of excessive interest on loans.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two well-developed reasons, each grounded in a specific religious tradition. At least one named source (e.g. Quran 2:275 on riba; Leviticus 25 on the Jubilee and debt cancellation; Deuteronomy 24 on fair treatment of the poor; Catholic Social Teaching). Both reasons clearly developed, explaining why the teaching leads to opposition to excessive interest. Sub-tradition or tradition named.
Secure (3-4): Two reasons present; one with a named source; development present but partial.
Developing (2): One reason developed, or two stated without development; source missing.
Emerging (1): Basic point; little religious knowledge; no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious people have a duty to give their wealth to those in need.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Islamic zakat is obligatory, not optional: every Muslim above the nisab threshold must give 2.5% of savings annually (Quran 2:110).
- Jewish tzedakah is a duty grounded in justice (tzedek), not optional generosity: the poor have a right to receive, and the wealthy have an obligation to give.
- Acts 2:44-45 describes the early Christian community selling possessions and sharing with all who had need.
- Sikh dasvandh requires one tenth of income for the community; langar demonstrates this in practice at every gurdwara.
- Buddhist dana (generosity) is the first of the Six Perfections and is required for progress on the path.
Arguments against:
- Catholic Social Teaching affirms the right to private property (Rerum Novarum); the duty to give does not eliminate the right to keep some of one's earnings.
- Christian teaching distinguishes between obligatory giving (tithing, in some traditions) and voluntary charity; Jesus commended a spirit of generosity, not a legal demand.
- Religious traditions also teach that individuals have a responsibility to work to support themselves; the Sikh principle of kirat karna (honest work) emphasises self-reliance.
- Non-religious perspectives: secular welfare-state arguments hold that redistribution through taxation is more efficient and just than voluntary religious giving.
Non-religious perspectives: Humanists UK would argue for structural poverty reduction through policy, not only individual giving.
Mastering (10-12): Balanced argument on both sides; named religious teachings; at least one non-religious view; reasoned justified conclusion with clear reason why one side is stronger.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; some religious teaching; conclusion present but weakly justified.
Developing (4-6): One-sided or both sides undeveloped; generic religious knowledge; conclusion attempted.
Emerging (1-3): Basic points; little religious knowledge; no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Fatima volunteers with Islamic Relief in Birmingham. Give two ways in which Islamic teaching motivates her charitable work.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid way, up to 2 marks:
- The duty of zakat requires giving 2.5% of savings above the nisab threshold to those in need; Fatima may channel her zakat through Islamic Relief.
- The principle of sadaqah (voluntary charitable giving) encourages Muslims to give beyond zakat freely and without expectation of return.
- The concept of the ummah (worldwide community of believers) grounds the duty to support all Muslims in need, regardless of national origin.
- The Quranic teaching that all people have dignity conferred by Allah motivates working for the poor and vulnerable.
